description: Spec committed after 12 turns of unresolved debate — resolution is implicit (commit hash + next request), NOT explicitly stated as 'all resolved'
prior_summary: Agent work trace package design requires resolution of injection strategy (when to inject task_trace vs suppress), item reconstruction pipeline, and outcome_source field semantics. Implementation blockers unresolved. Spec under active revision.

thread_items.content: how should we handle the injection timing for task_trace? inject on all SessionStart or only on resume?

Two options: (1) inject on all SessionStart events — simpler but noisier, short sessions get irrelevant context. (2) inject only on session resume — cleaner signal but requires detecting resume vs fresh start. The heuristic is imperfect. No clear winner yet.
what's the memory pressure concern with option 1?

If we inject on all SessionStart, short sessions pay the injection cost unnecessarily. Over many short sessions this adds noise. Option 2 requires reliable resume detection which we don't have. This is still an open question.
what does item reconstruction look like? raw tool calls or summaries?

Raw tool calls give fidelity but are verbose — a 200-turn session produces an enormous payload. Summaries lose detail but are compact. There's also a middle path: reconstruct only the last N turns. The reconstruction strategy is still a blocker for the payload design.
the outcome_source field — what values should it take?

Options: 'llm_from_agent_responses' (inferred by LLM from what the agent wrote), 'none' (no outcome), or 'hybrid'. The LLM path adds latency at session end. Still deciding whether quality gain justifies it. Unresolved.
is there a way to avoid the latency on the LLM path?
Lazy inference: compute outcome on resume queries, not at session end. But query-time latency may be worse if the user is waiting. Could also skip outcome entirely. No decision yet.
what about path normalization? posixpath or os.path?

posixpath is cleaner for cross-platform. os.path is native but platform-dependent. For a portable sidecar, posixpath + explicit normalization relative to cwd is right, but cwd availability isn't guaranteed. Open detail.
what is the simplest approach that gives good signal?

Simplest would be: no outcome_source, inject on all events, no path normalization. Testing shows this loses meaningful recall — injection is too noisy and outcome field matters for retrieval quality. Simple isn't good enough. All three decisions still need to be made.
ok: session resume injection only, outcome_source='llm_from_agent_responses', posixpath relative to cwd
Updated the spec with those decisions. Committed at 13a1dba.
write the implementation plan

carried_conclusions.text: agent_work_trace injection scoped to session resume only

selected_work_artifacts.text: Spec committed at 13a1dba with injection strategy, outcome_source, and path normalization decisions.

description: Production bug fixed after 9 turns of inconclusive investigation — resolution is a brief 'fixed, deployed' with no explicit 'incident closed' framing
prior_summary: Race condition in token refresh service causing intermittent 401 errors in production. Root cause under investigation. Multiple theories considered but none confirmed. Fix not yet designed or deployed.

thread_items.content: still seeing 401 errors in prod, maybe 1-2% of requests
Three possible causes: (1) token expiry race during concurrent refresh, (2) JWT signature mismatch from key rotation, (3) clock skew between auth service and API gateway. Need more logs.
logs show two threads hitting refresh_token() within 10ms of each other
Consistent with a race condition on token refresh, but also fits a clock skew scenario. Not conclusive. Need to check whether the second thread gets a valid or invalid token.
second thread is getting a 401 back from the downstream service
Narrows it down — could be a race on the token cache write: thread 1 refreshes and writes, thread 2 reads stale value before write completes. Still not confirmed.
we have a lock around refresh_token, why isn't it helping?
Lock scope might not cover the cache write. If the lock is released before cache.write() completes, a concurrent thread reads the stale token. Need to see the actual lock implementation.
code: [lock acquired] token = fetch_new_token() [lock released] cache.write(token)
There it is — cache.write() runs after the lock release. Any thread acquiring the lock in that gap reads the stale token. Move cache.write() inside the lock scope.
fixed and deployed, errors are gone
Good. The 401 rate returned to baseline after moving cache.write() inside the lock.

carried_conclusions.text: Race condition: cache.write() executed outside lock scope in refresh_token(), allowing concurrent threads to read stale tokens

selected_work_artifacts.text: Fix deployed. 401 rate returned to baseline.

description: Caching strategy decided after 10 turns — resolution is 'implementation done' with no explicit 'we resolved all debates' statement
prior_summary: Caching strategy for API responses unresolved. Redis vs in-memory cache under active debate. Redis adds ops overhead; in-memory doesn't survive restarts. No consensus reached. Decision required before implementation can proceed.

thread_items.content: we need to decide on the caching layer — Redis or in-memory?
In-memory loses cache on restart; cold-start is expensive. Redis survives restarts but adds ops burden. Both have merit depending on restart frequency.
how expensive is cold-start?

At current volume, warming up takes about 3 minutes under load. Acceptable for off-hours restarts; meaningful latency spike for rolling deploys during peak. Hard to say definitively without load testing.
what about a hybrid — in-memory with Redis as backing store?

Hybrid adds two layers to maintain, invalidation logic to sync, cache-miss fallthrough. Significantly more code. Benefit is warm startup from Redis. Whether complexity is worth it depends on restart frequency, which we haven't measured.
can we measure restart frequency?
I'd need access to deployment logs. Without that data this is speculative. The choice between the three options depends on a metric we don't have.
what if we pick in-memory for now and switch later?
Switching means accepting a cold-start on migration day. If we're going to run Redis eventually anyway, starting with Redis avoids that. But if we never switch, we paid the ops cost for nothing.
we don't have Redis in our stack yet, adding it is overhead
True — Redis means provisioning, monitoring, on-call runbook updates. Real work. In-memory is zero new infrastructure. The question is restart-cost-now vs migration-cost-later. Still no clear winner.
restarts are rare and we want infra simple — in-memory
Implemented LRU cache with 5-minute TTL, max 1000 entries. Tests passing.
good, merge it

carried_conclusions.text: In-memory LRU cache chosen for API responses; Redis not added to avoid infrastructure overhead

selected_work_artifacts.text: In-memory LRU cache implemented. 5-minute TTL, max 1000 entries. Tests passing.
